# Failure modes

Agents fail in recurring ways.  Most reports are anecdotes tied to one model version, so treat
the list as things to watch for, not as measured rates.

## Unverified success

- The agent reports that the work is done and correct when it is not.
- Signs: placeholder implementations, hardcoded values, and tests that were disabled, deleted, or rewritten to pass.
- Read the diff of the tests, not only the code.  Tell the agent to report a test it thinks is wrong rather than change it.
- See [Verify](03-workflows.qmd#explore-plan-implement-verify).

## Scope creep

- The agent adds things you did not ask for: extra features, abstractions for one-time use, defensive checks, comments on untouched code.
- Each addition is plausible on its own.  Together they make the diff hard to review.
- Add a rule to the [instructions file](02-context.qmd#instructions): "Only make changes that are directly requested or clearly necessary."

## Assumptions

- A vague prompt gets filled in with guesses, sometimes large ones, and the agent does not always say so.
- State what is out of scope, and ask the agent to list its assumptions before it starts.

## Repeated corrections

- Correcting the same mistake over and over in chat fills the context with failed attempts.
- After the second correction, `/clear` and rewrite the prompt.  If the mistake recurs across sessions, add a rule to the instructions file or a check the agent can run.

## Generated-code debt

- For code, keep your "AI slop" separate from anything curated or hand-written.  You can quickly rack up a lot of "technical debt".
  - I like having `project/src/experimental/` for Claude-generated stuff that I move into `project/src/some_file.py` .
  - Understanding the logic an agent implemented is almost always worthwhile.

## Fabricated references

See [Validating references](07-rp1-practices.qmd#validating-references).

## Over-long sessions

- A session that covers several unrelated tasks carries all of them in context.  See [Sessions](02-context.qmd#sessions).
- Long unsupervised runs drift.  One [report](https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/9/7/astra-why/) describes a 35-hour run that produced nothing usable.  Set a time limit and check intermediate output.

## What *doesn't* work well

- Work you cannot verify.  If there is no test, build, or reference result to check against, you are relying on the agent's own claim.
- Vague objectives such as "improve performance" or "clean this up".
- Security-sensitive and performance-critical code.  The output looks as confident as any other and still needs expert review.
- Visual checks.  Agents miss obvious layout and plotting bugs even when they look at a screenshot.
